title: Using MGCs to Stoke Student Work Ethic
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart connects his "Article of the Day" warm-up experiment to his September Invitation focus on tracking Moments of Genuine Connection, showing how a brief one-on-one check-in can be matched to exactly what a student's warm-up work reveals. He sorts student work into three buckets -- not doing the work at all, doing it without care, and doing it with real curiosity and endurance -- and models a distinct MGC script for each: a redirecting-but-affirming hallway pull-out for the first, a curious diagnostic conversation for the second, and an energizing celebration for the third. He notes that by week four, hallway pull-outs are normalized enough that students no longer read them as punishment, and that MGCs can't reach every disengaged student every day. Throughout, the underlying logic is that motivation grows out of students feeling seen, valued, and respected, and that matching the check-in's content to the specific work situation makes the MGC land more precisely than a generic pep talk would.
points: Stuart matches MGC scripts to three distinct student states -- not working, working without care, and working with real care -- arguing a one-size-fits-all check-in is less effective than one tuned to what the teacher is actually observing.
His script for the not-working conversation pairs high expectations with genuine care so the redirect doesn't read as punitive.

By week four, hallway pull-outs have been normalized enough that "everyone gets pulled out," which lowers the social cost of an individual check-in and makes the strategy sustainable across a whole class.

MGCs aren't a universal fix: Stuart is explicit that he can't reach every disengaged student every day, so for most off-task students he simply redirects and lingers until they begin -- reserving MGCs as a slow-and-steady strategy.
quotes: My whole methodology of student motivation was born out of a simple reality: students can only grow toward mastery if they 1) do work, and 2) do it with care.

Paden, I'm noticing that you're not working on the article. Is everything okay? What's getting in your way? Is there anything I can do to help? I'm having this conversation with you because I have high expectations, and I know you can reach them.

By this point in the school year (week 4), being pulled into the hallway for a brief MGC has been normalized. Students know that everyone gets pulled out, and the word on the street is that it can be a simple check-in.

MGCs aren't always possible for all kids at all times. This is a slow-and-steady strategy that reaps its fruits when we use it for one, two, or three kids a day, keeping track to make sure all kids get a moment every month or so.

Kaylin, when you ask those great questions during our article work, I've got to tell you: it is awesome. You're leading the charge of curiosity in this class, and the results of your questions are almost always more questions.
It's really important to look for these last kinds of MGCs because they feel amazing to both the student and to us teachers. Energy boosts all around — good stuff.
